source_spans.locator: Nature 377, published p.155, Abstract/opening: daily practice improves speed and accuracy for one rapid finger sequence; improvement does not generalize to a matched sequence or the opposite hand; two fMRI time scales are distinguished

Nature 377, published p.155, Fig. 1 and accompanying text: sequence A/B definitions, non-dominant-hand training, matched component movements, longitudinal behavioral performance, trained-versus-control and hand-specificity tests

Nature 377, published p.156, Methods/Fig. 2: six adult male imaging participants; 4-T imaging; alternating rest/sequence blocks; both sequences executed during scanning at the same fixed slow rate so movement components and rate are matched

Nature 377, published pp.156-157, Figs. 3-4 and text: pretraining M1 activation extent is comparable; early session shows order-dependent attenuation followed by reversal within the first session; effect is sequence-specific

Nature 377, published p.157, fast-phase interpretation: first-session paced repetition coincides with improved speed and accuracy; authors interpret the ordering-effect reversal as a short-timescale processing change

Nature 377, published p.157, slow-phase result: after about three weeks of daily practice, trained-sequence M1 activation extent is consistently larger than control irrespective presentation order; asymmetry persists at 10 and 21 weeks without additional training

Nature 377, published p.157, signal analysis/interpretation: mean signal-intensity change is similar for trained and control sequences, while some pixels respond only to the trained sequence; authors interpret this as expansion/recruitment of the trained representation

Nature 377, published pp.157-158, Discussion/conclusion: two phases are proposed—within-session acquisition-related change and slower between-session representational change; cortical reorganization is presented as a possible substrate for long-term retention, not a randomized causal manipulation

conditions: one five-element finger-opposition sequence was repeatedly practiced with the non-dominant hand, while a second sequence used the same component movements in a different order and was not practiced outside imaging sessions
behavioral specificity was assessed against the matched unpracticed sequence and against performance with the opposite hand
during imaging, trained and control sequences were executed at the same externally paced slow rate, matching movement rate and component movements while differing in prior practice history
within imaging sets, sequence order was varied so transient order effects could be separated from sequence-specific long-term differences
population: six adult male imaging participants aged 24-44 years, five right-handed and one left-handed
four additional adults contributed to the broader longitudinal behavioral performance sample
task: rapid five-element finger-opposition sequence performance during longitudinal practice
fixed-rate execution of trained and matched control sequences during repeated functional imaging sessions
temporal_scope: within the first imaging session over approximately 30 minutes of repeated paced execution
daily practice over several weeks, with the slow imaging difference established by approximately week 3-4
follow-up measurements months later, including 10- and 21-week observations without additional practice

nodes.description: repeated daily practice of one designated five-element sequence with the non-dominant hand
a second sequence composed of the same component finger movements in a different order and not practiced outside imaging sessions
behavioral test of whether the practice-related advantage transfers to the contralateral hand
30-second unpaced performance test in which completed sequences and errors are counted
number of correctly completed target sequences per 30-second performance interval
number of ordering errors during the 30-second performance interval
functional imaging during matched slow-rate execution of the trained and control sequences in alternating rest and movement blocks
whether a sequence is executed first or second within a repeated imaging set
number or spatial extent of source-defined M1 pixels showing task-linked blood-oxygenation signal change
magnitude of blood-oxygenation signal change in responding M1 pixels
source-described short-timescale processing regime indexed by reversal of the within-set ordering effect during the first session
source-inferred longer-timescale expansion or recruitment of cortical territory selective for the repeatedly practiced sequence
higher correctly completed sequence rate together with stable or reduced ordering errors

relations.description: extended practice increases the rate of correct sequence completion while accuracy is maintained or improved
the behavioral advantage is sequence-specific: the matched unpracticed sequence does not show the same improvement
testing with the opposite hand shows little or no transfer of the practice-related advantage
the unpaced 30-second performance probe supplies the behavioral rate and error outcomes
practice-related behavioral improvement is defined jointly by faster correct sequence production and nonworsening accuracy
the matched-rate imaging probe supplies spatial-extent and signal-amplitude outcomes while controlling execution rate and component movements

within the first session, repeating a sequence first produces an early transient reduction in activated extent, but later in the same session the ordering effect reverses; introducing a new sequence restores the earlier ordering pattern, supporting sequence specificity
the short-timescale ordering-effect change occurs within the initial session, before the slower trained-versus-control representational asymmetry that emerges after weeks of practice
after several weeks, the practiced sequence recruits a larger M1 activation extent than the matched control sequence regardless of within-set presentation order
the trained-versus-control extent asymmetry is retained at later follow-up observations months after practice has ceased
the long-term trained-versus-control difference is expressed primarily as spatial extent rather than a general increase in mean signal amplitude, which is reported as similar for the two sequences

the source interprets the selective spatial expansion as experience-dependent reorganization that may contribute to long-term retention; the imaging result itself does not establish a causal storage mechanism
